note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/07 Equilibria/7.2 Brønsted–Lowry theory of acids and bases.md
outline: Memorise the common acid and alkali formulas. A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton and a base accepts one. Strength describes extent of aqueous dissociation, not concentration. Neutralisation makes water and a salt. The starting pH, equivalence pH and steepness of a titration curve identify the acid–alkali pair and determine which indicator can locate its end point.

misconceptions.refutation: A formula identifies the substance, while strength depends on extent of dissociation.
misconceptions.contrast: A formula identifies the substance, while strength depends on extent of dissociation.

misconceptions.refutation: A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts a proton; an acid donates one.
misconceptions.contrast: A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts a proton; an acid donates one.

misconceptions.refutation: Weak means partially dissociated; dilute describes low concentration.
misconceptions.contrast: Weak means partially dissociated; dilute describes low concentration.

misconceptions.refutation: At equal analytical concentration a strong acid produces more hydrogen ions than a weak acid.
misconceptions.contrast: At equal analytical concentration a strong acid produces more hydrogen ions than a weak acid.

misconceptions.refutation: The ionic event is hydrogen ions reacting with hydroxide ions to give water; equivalence pH can differ from 7.
misconceptions.contrast: The ionic event is hydrogen ions reacting with hydroxide ions to give water; equivalence pH can differ from 7.

misconceptions.statement: Sulfur dioxide forms sulfate directly with calcium hydroxide
misconceptions.refutation: The first salt is calcium sulfite; forming sulfate would require oxidation.
misconceptions.contrast: The first salt is calcium sulfite; forming sulfate would require oxidation.

misconceptions.refutation: Weak acid and strong base give pH above 7; strong acid and weak base give pH below 7.
misconceptions.contrast: Weak acid and strong base give pH above 7; strong acid and weak base give pH below 7.

misconceptions.refutation: The transition interval must lie within the steep pH change near equivalence.
misconceptions.contrast: The transition interval must lie within the steep pH change near equivalence.

worked.problem: Sketch the curve when 0.10 mol dm$^{-3}$ ethanoic acid is titrated with 0.10 mol dm$^{-3}$ sodium hydroxide.

steps.do: Start below pH 7, but higher than a strong acid at the same concentration.
Show a buffer region followed by a steep rise with equivalence above pH 7.
Finish at high pH after excess alkali.

faded.problem: For hydrochloric acid titrated with sodium hydroxide, state the pH at the equivalence point at 298 K.

worked.problem: Select an indicator for ethanoic acid titrated with sodium hydroxide.

steps.do: Locate the equivalence point above pH 7.
steps.why: The conjugate base makes the solution alkaline.

steps.do: Choose phenolphthalein, whose transition lies within the steep rise.
steps.why: The end point then closely tracks equivalence.

faded.problem: For a strong acid–strong alkali titration, an indicator changes from pH 4 to pH 6. Calculate the width of its transition interval in pH units.

items.stem: Equal volumes of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid are at the same temperature. Their pH values are measured using a pH meter. Identical freshly cleaned magnesium strips are then added to separate samples of each acid. Explain which acid has the lower pH and which gives the faster initial rate of hydrogen evolution. Relate both comparisons to dissociation and hydrogen-ion concentration.

rubric.point: Hydrochloric acid is fully dissociated in aqueous solution, whereas ethanoic acid is only partially dissociated.
At the same acid concentration, hydrochloric acid has a higher hydrogen-ion concentration.
A pH meter gives a lower pH for hydrochloric acid than for ethanoic acid because its hydrogen-ion concentration is higher.
Magnesium initially produces hydrogen faster in hydrochloric acid because the higher hydrogen-ion concentration gives more frequent successful collisions at the metal surface.

items.explanation: Hydrochloric acid is fully dissociated in aqueous solution, whereas ethanoic acid is only partially dissociated. At the same acid concentration, hydrochloric acid has a higher hydrogen-ion concentration. A pH meter gives a lower pH for hydrochloric acid than for ethanoic acid because its hydrogen-ion concentration is higher. Magnesium initially produces hydrogen faster in hydrochloric acid because the higher hydrogen-ion concentration gives more frequent successful collisions at the metal surface.
hints: Compare full and partial dissociation at equal acid concentration.
Relate hydrogen-ion concentration to the pH-meter reading.
Relate hydrogen-ion concentration to the initial reaction rate at identical magnesium surfaces.

rubric.point: Label every vertical axis pH and every horizontal axis volume of alkali added.

items.explanation: B is correct. In NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O, NH₄⁺ donates a proton and acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid. On the damp litmus paper, NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻: water donates a proton to ammonia and also acts as an acid. The hydroxide ions turn red litmus blue. A is wrong because water is a proton donor here, not a base; C and D wrongly classify ammonium as a base. The two acids act in separate reactions.

At 298 K, titration A adds aqueous ammonia to hydrochloric acid; titration B adds sodium hydroxide to ethanoic acid. Each flask initially contains $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ acid, and both alkalis have concentration $0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$. (a) Sketch the two pH curves with labelled axes, starting pH, direction, steep region, equivalence volume and equivalence pH relative to 7, and final alkaline region. Exact pH values are not required. (b) Explain the equivalence pH differences and label B's buffer region with the species responsible.

rubric.point: Label both vertical axes pH and both horizontal axes volume of alkali added / $\mathrm{cm^3}$.
Both curves rise as alkali is added to acid.
A starts at approximately pH 1; B starts acidic but at a higher pH (about 3).
Both show a steep rise near $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of alkali added.
A has equivalence below pH 7 because ammonium ions donate protons to water.
B has equivalence above pH 7 because ethanoate ions accept protons from water, producing hydroxide ions.
B has a buffer region before equivalence, containing ethanoic acid and ethanoate ions.
After equivalence both are alkaline; B approaches a higher final pH because its excess alkali is strong.

items.explanation: Both curves rise because alkali is added to acid, and equal amounts of monoprotic acid require the same equivalence volume. Ammonium ions make A acidic at equivalence, whereas ethanoate ions make B alkaline. Before equivalence, B contains both weak acid and its conjugate base, so its buffer region resists pH change.

items.stem: An acid is titrated by adding alkali. Around equivalence, one small addition makes the pH rise from 7.5 to 10.5; outside this interval the pH changes gradually. Select an indicator and justify your choice using both intervals and the sharpness of the end point. Explain why the other indicator is unsuitable and whether it changes colour before or after equivalence.

rubric.point: Phenolphthalein is suitable.
Its entire pH 8.2–10.0 transition lies within the steep pH 7.5–10.5 interval.
A small added volume then produces the full colour change, giving a sharp end point near equivalence.
Methyl orange is unsuitable: pH 3.1–4.4 lies below the steep interval, so it changes colour too early, before equivalence.

items.explanation: The entire phenolphthalein transition lies inside the steep interval, so a small change in volume produces a clear colour change near equivalence. Methyl orange changes below that interval, before equivalence, and would give too small a titre.
hints: Compare the whole transition interval of each indicator with the data for the curve.
A sharp end point requires the full colour change to occur over a small added volume.
Track the pH from low to high to decide when each transition is reached.

9701-7.2.5.motivate: How can you recognise and use water in an exam question?
9701-7.2.5.establish: At 298 K, pure water has pH 7. An acidic solution has pH below 7; an alkaline solution has pH above 7.
9701-7.2.5.connect: Connect this idea to acidic and the acid–base reactions around it.
9701-7.2.5.note:
- water: At 298 K, pure water has pH 7. An acidic solution has pH below 7; an alkaline solution has pH above 7.
- Check the role or observation involving acidic.
9701-7.2.5.self_explain: Explain how water relates to acidic.

9701-7.2.6.motivate: How can you recognise and use pH meter in an exam question?
9701-7.2.6.establish: At equal concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH, greater conductivity and a faster initial reaction with the same reactive metal than a weak acid. Use a pH meter, universal indicator, conductivity meter or the rate of hydrogen evolution.
9701-7.2.6.connect: Connect this idea to universal indicator and the acid–base reactions around it.
9701-7.2.6.note:
- pH meter: At equal concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH, greater conductivity and a faster initial reaction with the same reactive metal than a weak acid. Use a pH meter, universal indicator, conductivity meter or the rate of hydrogen evolution.
- Check the role or observation involving universal indicator.

9701-7.2.7.motivate: How can you recognise and use neutralisation in an exam question?
9701-7.2.7.establish: Neutralisation occurs when $\ce{H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) -> H2O (l)}$. The acid supplies hydrogen ions and the alkali supplies hydroxide ions.
9701-7.2.7.connect: Connect this idea to hydrogen ion and the acid–base reactions around it.
9701-7.2.7.note:
- neutralisation: Neutralisation occurs when $\ce{H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) -> H2O (l)}$. The acid supplies hydrogen ions and the alkali supplies hydroxide ions.
- Check the role or observation involving hydrogen ion.
9701-7.2.7.self_explain: Explain how neutralisation relates to hydrogen ion.

9701-7.2.8.motivate: How can you recognise and use salt in an exam question?
9701-7.2.8.establish: Neutralisation forms a salt as well as water: $\ce{HCl (aq) + NaOH (aq) -> NaCl (aq) + H2O (l)}$. The salt contains the acid anion and the base cation.
9701-7.2.8.connect: Connect this idea to acid anion and the acid–base reactions around it.
9701-7.2.8.note:
- salt: Neutralisation forms a salt as well as water: $\ce{HCl (aq) + NaOH (aq) -> NaCl (aq) + H2O (l)}$. The salt contains the acid anion and the base cation.
- Check the role or observation involving acid anion.
9701-7.2.8.self_explain: Explain how salt relates to acid anion.

9701-7.2.9.motivate: How can you recognise and use strong acid–strong alkali in an exam question?
9701-7.2.9.establish: Sketch pH against volume of alkali added to acid. Strong acid–strong alkali has a steep jump centred at pH 7; weak acid–strong alkali starts at higher pH and has equivalence above 7; strong acid–weak alkali has equivalence below 7; weak acid–weak alkali has no sharp jump. Reverse trends when acid is added to alkali.
9701-7.2.9.connect: Connect this idea to weak acid–strong alkali and the acid–base reactions around it.
9701-7.2.9.note:
- strong acid–strong alkali: Sketch pH against volume of alkali added to acid. Strong acid–strong alkali has a steep jump centred at pH 7; weak acid–strong alkali starts at higher pH and has equivalence above 7; strong acid–weak alkali has equivalence below 7; weak acid–weak alkali has no sharp jump. Reverse trends when acid is added to alkali.
- Check the role or observation involving weak acid–strong alkali.
9701-7.2.9.self_explain: Explain how strong acid–strong alkali relates to weak acid–strong alkali.

9701-7.2.10.motivate: How can you recognise and use indicator range in an exam question?
9701-7.2.10.establish: Select an indicator whose colour-change pH range lies in the steep part of the titration curve around equivalence. For strong acid–strong alkali, several indicators work; weak acid–strong alkali favours phenolphthalein; strong acid–weak alkali favours methyl orange; weak–weak gives no sharp visual end point.
9701-7.2.10.connect: Connect this idea to steep change and the acid–base reactions around it.
9701-7.2.10.note:
- indicator range: Select an indicator whose colour-change pH range lies in the steep part of the titration curve around equivalence. - Check the role or observation involving steep change.
